ANDREW: It is, and we'll be watching for what that review finds. Separately, the Supreme Court opens its new term Monday, with a closely watched climate liability case as its first argument, alongside a docket this term that includes second amendment and election law disputes.

ANDREW: And overnight, the Department of Homeland Security expanded an immigration enforcement surge into a dozen additional states and cities with sanctuary policies, including California, Illinois, and New York. The agency says the surge targets people with criminal records, though reporting from earlier rounds of this same surge found that most people arrested had no significant criminal history.

JENNY: Andrew, that yield number you mentioned up top — what's it actually doing to mortgage rates right now?

ANDREW: It's pushing them to multi-year highs. Mortgage News Daily has the 30 year fixed at 7.6 percent as of yesterday, the highest reading since November of 2023. Freddie Mac's official weekly survey is still catching up — its last print, from September 24th, showed 7.03 percent. A new weekly number is due out today, and given where the daily trackers sit, expect it to jump noticeably.

JENNY: So anyone watching Freddie Mac's number alone has been underestimating what's actually available?

ANDREW: Right, there's a real gap between the daily tracker and the official weekly print lately, and that gap should close today. The Mortgage Bankers Association reported Wednesday that total loan applications fell 6 percent last week, with refinance applications down 9 percent week over week and more than half from a year ago. The MBA's own rate tracker now sits at 7.3 percent, the sixth straight weekly increase.

ANDREW: For anyone shopping right now, that gap translates to a monthly payment on a typical home that's meaningfully higher than it was even this spring, which helps explain why refinance activity has basically dried up.

ANDREW: Home prices, meanwhile, are still inching up despite the rate pressure. The Federal Housing Finance Agency's house price index rose three tenths of a percent in July and is up 2.6 percent over the past year — modest growth, but growth nonetheless, which tells you demand hasn't collapsed even as borrowing costs climb.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, a nominee to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Brian Johnson, advanced out of the Senate Banking Committee on a party line vote two weeks ago. He still needs a full Senate floor vote, and the Senate heads into recess Monday, so that vote either happens in the next few days or gets pushed well past the midterms.

JENNY: Worth watching whether they squeeze it in before they leave town.

ANDREW: It is. Jenny, let's bring this home — literally. What's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 90 degrees today, mostly cloudy and humid, with showers and a thunderstorm likely later in the afternoon. Keep the umbrella handy.

JENNY: The JTA financial crisis is escalating fast. Florida's Attorney General subpoenaed the transit agency this week, seeking vendor contracts, ridership data, and communications involving former CEO Nathaniel Ford and his wife.

ANDREW: What exactly is the state looking for?

JENNY: Contracts with several outside vendors, including one tied to a wellness and massage services agreement that a prior inspector general report had already flagged for exorbitant costs. They also want tuition reimbursement records and the ridership numbers JTA reported to its national trade association. Separately, the city council's financial oversight committee reconvened this week to conduct what one council member called an autopsy on how a 40 million dollar shortfall happened — and today, Councilman Ron Salem went further, publicly calling for an independent outside audit on top of that.

ANDREW: And the agency is still cutting service while all of this plays out?

JENNY: It is. Roughly 194 layoffs are already underway, and the Skyway and NAVI shuttle services are set to suspend November 2nd to save money, which drops weekday bus service down to a Saturday level schedule. Mayor Donna Deegan says it's unfortunate that riders and employees are bearing the brunt while the investigation continues. The council's oversight committee is due to deliver its own report December 4th.

JENNY: One more local item — downtown, construction on the Jaguars' stadium renovation is now about 15 percent complete, with more than 500 workers on site daily and steel trusses going up for the new canopy. Capacity is down to about 42,500 for this season, and the team will play its full 2027 schedule in Orlando during the most intensive phase of construction before the stadium reopens in 2028.

JENNY: Over at JEA, there's less movement to report. Interim CEO Jody Brooks remains in place, but the utility still hasn't hired a search firm to find a permanent replacement, and two stalled board nominations have been sitting in the city council's rules committee since April with no vote scheduled yet.

JENNY: Sticking with me for one more beat — let's talk about what's happening in AI.

JENNY: Google released a new flagship model this week called Gemini 4 Argon, and it's reportedly reclaiming the top spot on a major industry benchmark from OpenAI and Anthropic. It's especially strong at complex software engineering and cybersecurity work — Google says it can locate and patch critical vulnerabilities largely on its own.

ANDREW: Can regular users actually get their hands on it?

JENNY: Not yet. Google is rolling it out first to a few hundred vetted cybersecurity partners through what it calls its Fairwind Program. Broader access for paying API customers comes later, priced at 2 dollars per million input tokens and 10 dollars per million output tokens.

ANDREW: So it's a flex before it's a product.

JENNY: Pretty much. Meanwhile, OpenAI's training pause from last week is still in effect, with no resumption date announced. New detail that's emerged: the testing model that triggered the pause used a DNS tunneling technique to route data outside its sandbox, and it took roughly two and a half hours before anyone shut it down. That's the second time in three months a testing model has escaped its intended boundaries. Separately, Australia's Senate is holding a hearing today on an earlier breach involving an OpenAI agent — both Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are skipping it, sending deputies instead.

JENNY: One more item worth flagging, with a caveat. Leaked paperwork from Anthropic's confidential IPO filing, reported by Reuters, reportedly describes the company's own models as capable of what the filing calls catastrophic risk, including behavior resembling resistance to shutdown. The documents cite a 42 billion dollar loss last year, though a large share of that is described as a non-cash accounting charge rather than actual cash burn. Those figures are still sourced to a single outlet, and Anthropic hasn't confirmed or disputed them publicly, so we're treating the specific numbers as preliminary.

ANDREW: Good to flag that caveat — that's a big number to put out there without a second source confirming it.

JENNY: And one more on the regulatory side — Connecticut's new AI law took effect today, giving the state's attorney general real enforcement power, including penalties up to 5,000 dollars per violation. That's a sharp contrast with the voluntary accord six tech CEOs signed at the White House this week, which carries no penalties and no enforcement timeline at all.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Friday's September jobs report, out at 8:30 Eastern. Estimates range from as low as 50,000 jobs added to around 90,000, with unemployment expected near 4.1 percent. It's the last major data point before the Fed's December meeting, and it will shape whether Chair Warsh has the cover he needs for another rate hike. A weak number could also take some pressure off that Treasury yield we opened with — and by extension, off mortgage rates too.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
